title: The Gita in the people's language
hookLine: the Gita, carried out of Sanskrit and into the language of the street
carry: God's word belongs in everyone's own tongue
tomorrow: The wall that met the tiger

cards: A temple in a small town by a river. A young man sits near a stone pillar and talks, verse by verse, through the Bhagavad Gita.

Not in Sanskrit, the language of the priests, but in Marathi, the language of the farmers, the potters, the women at the well, the people sitting in front of him. Beside him, someone writes every word down.
Those talks become a book that people in Maharashtra still read aloud together.

teach.b: Tradition says this happened at Nevasa, and that the man writing was Sachchidananda. The book is the Jnaneshwari, and it isn't a translation in the usual sense.
It walks through the Gita verse by verse and opens each one up with pictures from ordinary life.

teach.h: THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.
teach.b: Take the Gita's line about the person of steady wisdom, who draws the senses in the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. Jnaneshwar lingers there, so a farmer or a potter could see it.
The outcast boy of Paithan takes a teaching most people met in Sanskrit, a language few of his listeners had studied, and opens it in everyday Marathi.
He even promises to make his words so sweet they'd win a wager against nectar: a bet that the language of the street can carry the deepest things. Hindus took that bet.

teach.h: GOD'S WORD, IN YOUR OWN TONGUE.
teach.b: It's a real conviction of the bhakti saints: God's word is for everyone, in their own tongue.
It's why the Gita, the Ramayana and the saints' songs live on in Marathi, Tamil, Hindi, Bengali and many other languages, and why families read them aloud together.
Varkari groups still read the Jnaneshwari aloud, and sing its words on pilgrimage. And all through the book, Jnaneshwar hands the credit to his teacher, Nivritti, who is also his older brother.
The boldest claim about language, and the smallest about himself.

how: Varkari devotees read the Jnaneshwari aloud in groups, at home and in temples, and many read it along the way on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

games.q: you're Jnaneshwar. you've been shut out by the scholars, and you know the Gita well. what do you do with it?
o: argue with the scholars in Sanskrit until they accept you.
open it, verse by verse, in Marathi for anyone who'll listen.
games.why: he speaks it in Marathi, with pictures from daily life. the bhakti saints held that God's word is for everyone, in their own tongue.

practice: The Gita gives a picture you can try: the tortoise, drawing its limbs in. Sit, and one by one draw your attention in, from what you see, then what you hear, then the itch to check your phone, the way the tortoise pulls in each leg.

Rest there a few breaths. Then think of who first put something holy into plain words for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, say their name to yourself, once.

wordCard.voice: Jnaneshwar. The Marathi saint whose Jnaneshwari opened the Bhagavad Gita, verse by verse, in the language people spoke at home.

orig.note: Marathi, in Devanagari: the name of Jnaneshwar's book on the Bhagavad Gita.
